This article helps you find lists of mountains in Britain and Ireland. These lists are organized by how tall the mountains are (their height) and how much they stand out from the land around them (their prominence).
Height and prominence are the most important ways to sort mountains. A group called the UIAA uses these measurements to classify mountains. This list comes from the _Database of British and Irish Hills_ (DoBIH). It includes peaks that are at least 600 metres (1,969 ft) tall. It also only includes peaks that rise at least 30 metres (98 ft) above the land around them.
Because of these rules, this list includes 2,756 mountains called "Simms" in the British Isles (as of October 2022). Some mountain groups only count peaks with a prominence of 150 metres (492 ft) or more as true mountains. But using the 30 metres (98 ft) prominence rule gives us the biggest possible list of mountains.
If you want to see lists of mountains with a higher prominence, you can check out:
*   List of Marilyns in the British Isles: These mountains have a prominence of over 150 metres (492 ft).  
*   List of P600 mountains in the British Isles: These mountains have a prominence of over 600 metres (1,969 ft).

## What are Simms?
Even though the "Simms" list uses a lower prominence rule (30 metres (98 ft)), almost all famous Scottish mountains called "Munros" are included. For example, 281 out of 282 Munros are Simms. The only one missing is Maoile Lunndaidh, because its prominence changed to only 11 metres (36 ft) in 2014.
As of October 2018, the list of 2,754 British Isles Simms included:
*   281 of the 282 Munros.  
*   All 222 Corbetts.  
*   All 219 Grahams.  
*   All 118 Scottish New Donalds.  
*   All 524 of the England, Wales, and Ireland Hewitts.  
*   All 120 of the "major" mountains (called P600) in the British Isles.

## How Mountains are Measured
The lists of mountains are based on information from the DoBIH. Measuring how much a mountain stands out (its prominence) is tricky. It needs a detailed survey of the mountain's shape, not just its highest point. Because of this, these lists can change over time as new surveys are done.
Regional Top: This means it's the highest mountain in England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland, or the Isle of Man.

## Mountain Classifications
The DoBIH uses special codes for different types of mountains and hills. Here are some of the main ones:
*   Ma: Marilyn (prominence over 150m)  
*   Sim: Simm (height over 600m, prominence over 30m)  
*   M: Munro (Scottish mountains over 914.4m)  
*   C: Corbett (Scottish mountains between 762m and 914.4m)  
*   G: Graham (Scottish mountains between 609.6m and 762m)  
*   Hew: Hewitt (mountains in England, Wales, and Ireland over 609.6m)  
*   W: Wainwright (popular hills in the Lake District)  
*   A: Arderin (Irish mountains over 500m)  
*   P600: P600 (mountains with prominence over 600m)

## People Who Have Climbed All Mountains
It's a huge challenge to climb all the mountains in a certain group! As of December 31, 2021, 7,098 people had climbed all 282 Scottish Munros. As of April 2020, eleven people had climbed all 1556 Marilyns in Great Britain.
Even fewer people have climbed all the Simms. As of October 2022, only five people had climbed all 2532 Simms in Great Britain:
*   Ken Whyte (finished September 21, 2010)  
*   Iain Thow (finished June 7, 2015)  
*   Michael Earnshaw (finished July 16, 2019)  
*   Rob Woodall (finished June 28, 2021)  
*   Anne Bunn (finished September 24, 2022)
The first three people on this list have also climbed the Irish Simms, meaning they have climbed all the Simms in the entire British Isles!

## About Ben Nevis
No land anywhere within 739 km rises higher than the summit of Ben Nevis, which sits at the western end of the Grampians in Lochaber, just outside Fort William. It is the high point of Scotland, the United Kingdom and the British Isles alike, and around 150,000 people come each year — roughly three in four of them by the Mountain Track out of Glen Nevis.
The other face of the hill is the north face, whose cliffs reach some 700 metres and rank among the tallest in Scotland. They carry scrambles and rock routes across the full range of difficulty, and are the country's principal ice-climbing ground. The Charles Inglis Clark Memorial Hut, a private alpine hut, gives a view of them. A foot race has been run on the mountain since 1898.

## Welcome to Ben Nevis
Welcome to Ben Nevis, the largest mountain in the British Isles. Every year, over 150,000 people from all over the world, make their attempt to climb to the top and summit this majestic mountain. With the summit being 1,345m above sea level, it’s a climb that will test your abilities, strength and endurance.
We cover the different locations where you can park your car near Ben Nevis.
Ranging from easy to difficult there are a few options for those looking to push their abilities.
Looking for somewhere to stay during your visit near Ben Nevis? Here are some accommodation offerings.

## Explore The Surrounding Area
While Ben Nevis is the beating heart that attracts visitors from all over the world, the local area of Glen Nevis provides lots of other activities and things to do
Open
Open
Open

## Explore The Surrounding Area
#### Did You Know?
Ben Nevis or _Beinn Nibheis_ in Scottish Gaelic
Around 350 million years ago, a period of intense volcanic activity began, which resulted in the formation of the Scottish Highlands. The magma that erupted from the Earth’s crust cooled and solidified to form igneous rocks like granite, which make up the core of Ben Nevis.
Over millions of years, the surrounding softer sedimentary rock eroded away, leaving the harder granite exposed and forming the distinctive shape of the mountain.

## Most Asked Questions
##### How long will it take me to climb Ben Nevis?
This is dependent on your fitness levels. As a rough guide, we state the average person climbing via the mountain track, can do the climb in roughly 3 1/2 to 4 1/2 hours, during the summer months. It will vary though depending on weather conditions, how many rest breaks you take etc.

## Most Asked Questions
##### Are there toilets on Ben Nevis?
There are no toilet facilities on Ben Nevis. The Ben Nevis Visitor Centre offers toilet facilities but these are only open when the visitor centre is open itself. Opening hours vary throughout the year.

## Hear From Our Visitors
Creating lifelong memories, pushing boundaries and witnessing some of the most breathtaking views in Scotland are just a few of the many reasons people flock to Ben Nevis each year.
"Great walking country with magnificent views of the mountains. Well maintained paths certainly help with the walking.

## People Who Have Climbed All Mountains
It's a huge challenge to climb all the mountains in a certain group! As of December 31, 2021, 7,098 people had climbed all 282 Scottish Munros. As of April 2020, eleven people had climbed all 1556 Marilyns in Great Britain.
Even fewer people have climbed all the Simms. As of October 2022, only five people had climbed all 2532 Simms in Great Britain:
*   Ken Whyte (finished September 21, 2010)  
*   Iain Thow (finished June 7, 2015)  
*   Michael Earnshaw (finished July 16, 2019)  
*   Rob Woodall (finished June 28, 2021)  
*   Anne Bunn (finished September 24, 2022)
The first three people on this list have also climbed the Irish Simms, meaning they have climbed all the Simms in the entire British Isles!

Mountains of Wales
The Welsh mountains that make our landscapes so distinctive were carved out in the Ice Age, some 10,000 years ago. They’re our defence and our lifeline, a challenge and an inspiration. Their peaks, slopes and views are endlessly exciting to explore.

## Eryri
Rocky, rough and tough – that's how we like our mountains. Don’t think that just because you can take a train to the top,Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)isn't a proper peak. In fact,Eryri (Snowdonia) National Parkis a mountain and adventure capital that's up there with the classic Alpine destinations.
Each of the six official eight-mile routes to the highest mountain in Wales(1085m) offer sensational hiking and incredible views. In Eryri's nine ranges, there are 15 peaks over 900m high, including Yr Wyddfa itself. You may have heard of some of the others.Tryfan (918m) is a famous landmark:a triangular peak offering some of the best scrambling – and views – in Britain. Meanwhile, Cader Idris is 893m high and rears up from the shores of the beautiful Mawddach Estuary.

## Cambrian Mountains
The Cambrian Mountains is a name that describes the sparsely-populated landscape from Foel Fadian (563m) near Penfforddlas and Pumlumon Fawr (752m) near Ponterwyd in the north, all the way south through the Elenydd and the Elan Valley to Mynydd Mallaen (462m) near Llanymddyfri (Llandovery).At its southernmost tip you’ll discover Mynydd Llanfihangel-rhos-y-corn (356m) near Brechfa Forest. The Cambrian Mountains span the three counties of Powys, Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire.
Located between Eryri and the Bannau Brycheiniog (the Brecon Beacons), the Cambrian Mountains include cairned summits, open moorland and lush valleys. They are home to the sources of the rivers Wye and the Severn and the peaceful Elan Valley reservoirs.
By day walk some local and National Trails, journey on your mountain bike or horse and even paraglide from quiet nearby peaks. By night you will discover some of the darkest skies in Europe by visiting the many Dark Sky Discovery Sites on the Cambrian Mountains Astro Trail.

## Black Mountain Range, the Black Mountains, Fforest Fawr, and the Bannau Brycheiniog
The Black Mountain Range and the Black Mountains aren’t one and the same, although they are both found within the grassy expanses of theBannau Brycheiniog National Park. The Black Mountain Range, sometimes just called Black Mountain, is to the west, north of Swansea. It’s one of Wales’ most wild and remote corners with impressive, glacier-carved escarpments and isolated lakes, several miles from the nearest road. Its highest peak is Fan Brycheiniog (802m).
The Black Mountains are to the east, on the border with England. Y Fenni (Abergavenny), Y Gelli Gandryll (Hay-on-Wye), Llangorse, and the Monmouthshire & Brecon Canal stand at their feet, and their highest point is the Waun Fach plateau (811m). Confusingly enough, this range is also home to a peak called Black Mountain.
To the southwest isFforest Fawr(Great Forest), an upland area of remarkable limestone cliffs and caves. It was the the first Geopark in Wales.
Dominating the centre of the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park are the Bannau Brycheiniog, whose most celebrated peaks, Pen y Fan (886m) and Cribyn (795m), are the highest in southern Britain. The Bannau Brycheiniog are popular, with plenty of footpaths and bridleways. But they’re quieter than Eryri. Head off on foot and at times it can feel as if you have an entire mountainside to yourself.

## Be safe!


## Useful information
*   Download the Y Marilyns app– find a recommended starting point a short route description and background information for Welsh hills and mountains which are 150m or more higher than the surrounding land (this is classed as a ‘Marilyn’).The app is free to download and is run by volunteers from the Relative Hills Society.  
*   Traveline Cymruis a useful public transport journey planner.  
*   There are a number of apps and online maps where you can to find the location of electric vehicle charging points across Wales.SeveralNational Trustproperties across Wales have EV charging points.  
*   Help Wales become the first Refill Nation by using nearby Refill Points to fill up your water bottle before you head off. Find out more, including how todownload the free Refill appto find your nearest Refill Point on theRefill Return website.

Here you'll discover just some of the large selection of Welsh mountains. A list of 10 of the most magnificent peaks and mountain ranges in Wales. Also included is a short list of some noteworthy Welsh hills.

###


## Top 10 Mountains of Wales
1.    Yr Wyddfa – 1,085 m (3,559 ft)  
2.    Pen y Fan – 886 m (2,906 ft)  
3.    Carnedd Llewelyn – 1064 m (3,490 ft)  
4.    Glyder Fawr – 1,000 m (3,280 ft)  
5.    Tryfan – 917 m (3,008 ft)  
6.    Cadair Idris – 893 m (2,929 ft)  
7.    Waun Fach – 811 m (2,660 ft)  
8.    Fan Brycheiniog – 802 m (2,631 ft)  
9.    Plynlimon – 752 m (2,467 ft)  
10.    Foel Cwmcerwyn – 536 m (1,758 ft)

## How many mountains are there in Wales?
Wales is well-known for its mountainous terrain. But just how many mountains are there in Wales altogether? Although Wales is a small country covering just over 8,000 square miles, it’s famous for its numerous beautiful mountains – many of which were created during the last Ice Age approximately 12,000 years ago.
There are several mountain ranges here, spread across 13 regions. Within these ranges, there are a grand total of 136 mountains over 600 m (2,000 ft) high, and many more which don’t reach those lofty heights! Some of Wales’ most beloved hills are the Garn Boduan, the Mynydd Llangyndeyrn, Mynydd Dinas, Bryn Arw, and Mynydd Anelog.
**Fun fact:** The definition of a mountain is a rise which is 600m or, 2000ft above sea level. Mountains of this height are also known as ‘Hewitts’ in the United Kingdom. There are 525 Hewitts altogether in the UK.

## The Welsh 3000s
There are 15 mountains in Wales that stand at 914 m (3,000 ft) or more, these are called The Welsh 3000s. All 15 of them are located in Eryri National Park, within The Snowdon Massif, The Glyderau, and The Carneddau ranges.
The 15 peaks are:

## The Welsh 3000s
1.   Yr Wyddfa, The Snowdon Massif – 1,064 m (3,559 ft​)  
2.   Garnedd Ugain, The Snowdon Massif – 1,064 (3,494 ft)  
3.   Carnedd Llewelyn, The Carneddau – 1,063 m (3,490 ft)  
4.   Carnedd Dafydd, The Carneddau – 1,043 m (3,425 ft)  
5.   Glyder Fawr, The Glyderau – 1,001 m (3,284 ft)  
6.   Glyder Fach, The Glyderau – 994 m (3,261 ft)  
7.   Pen yr Ole Wen, The Carneddau – 977 m (3,208 ft)  
8.   Foel Grach, The Carneddau – 975 m (3,202 ft)  
9.   Yr Elen, The Carneddau – 961 m (3,156 ft)  
10.   Y Garn, The Glyderau – 946 m (3,106 ft)  
11.   Foel-fras, The Carneddau – 941 m (3,090 ft)  
12.   Garnedd Uchaf, The Carneddau – 925 m (3,038 ft)  
13.   Elidir Fawr, The Glyderau – 923 m (3,031 ft)  
14.   Crib Goch, The Snowdon Massif – 922 m (3,028 ft)  
15.   Tryfan, The Glyderau – 917 m (3,011 ft)
Due to the mountains’ proximity to each other, many avid climbers like to take on the challenge of visiting all 15 in one trip. This challenge is known as the Welsh 3000s Challenge. It requires embarking on a 50 km journey with almost 4000 m of ascent!

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
The highest mountain in Wales is Snowdon, Yr Wyddfa in Welsh, and it is located in the Eryri National Park. It stands at 1085 m (3,559 ft) high. The peak features at number one on the list of 15 Welsh mountains called the Welsh 3,000s (mountains over 914 m (3,000 ft).
All 15 of Wales’ highest mountains are part of the Eryri National Park region, but there are other mountainous regions that are home to some of the most fantastic mountains in Wales.
Check out the Welsh mountains list below to find out more about Wales’ mountainous regions.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 1. Snowdon, or Yr Wyddfa (Eryri National Park)
‘Yr Wyddfa’ is Wales’ highest mountain, standing at an incredible 1085 m (3559 ft) high! The peak is also one of Wales’ most famous landmarks, located in Eryri National Park, North Wales.
There are five main ranges within the National Park, these include the Snowdon massif itself as well the following:
*   Glyderau

*   Carneddau

*   Moelwynion

*   Moel Hebog
Wales’ highest mountains can be found within the Snowdon massif, Glyderau and Carneddau. Other ranges situated within the wider National Park are the Rhinogydd and the Cadair Idris and Aran Fawddwy ranges.
‘Yr Wyddfa’ was formed over millions of years, following numerous volcanic eruptions and glaciers forming and melting. The mountain is home to a rare flower called The Snowdon Lily, thought to have been around since the end of the Ice Age! It is the only known location in the UK that this flower has been spotted.
Hikers can choose from six eight-mile trails, of mixed difficulty, to reach the summit. However, the location is so popular, there is a train that can take visitors to the top where they will also find a visitor centre called Hafod Eryri.
The first recorded successful climb to the top of the mountain was by a man named Thomas Johnson in 1639.
Fun fact: ‘Yr Wyddfa’ is so high, that you can see across the sea to Ireland when standing at the summit!

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 2. Pen y Fan (Brecon Beacons)
Another incredibly popular peak in Wales is Pen y Fan (meaning ‘Top of the Beacons’ in English), situated in the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park. Standing at 886 m (2,906 ft) high, it is the highest mountain in South Wales.
In fact, the landmark is so popular among hikers and tourists that the mountain and surrounding area are owned and maintained by the National Trust. The organisation works to prevent erosion caused by walkers due to its popularity.
The mountain is also used in military training exercises as part of the selection process for the UK’s Special Forces.
The Brecon Beacons are home to some of the most loved mountains in Britain. There are six main peaks:
*   Pen y Fan – 886 m (2,906 ft)  
*   Corn Du – 873 m (2,864 ft)  
*   Cribyn – 795 m (2,608 ft)  
*   Waun Rydd – 769 m (2,522 ft)  
*   Bwlch y Ddwyallt – 754 m (2,473 ft)  
*   Fan y Bîg – 719 m (2,358 ft)
Fun fact: Pen y Fan and Corn Du, also known as the twin summits, were once referred to as Cadair Arthur or 'Arthur's Seat' after the Welsh legend, King Arthur.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 3. Carnedd Llywelyn (Eryri National Park)
Standing at 1064 m (3,490 ft), Carnedd Llywelyn is the highest point of the Carneddau range in Eryri.
You’ll find the summit located between two other mountains, Carnedd Dafydd and Foel Grach as well as cliffs for climbing including Craig yr Ysfa and the ‘Black Ladders’ of Ysgolion Duon.
Climbing Carnedd Llewelyn requires a long, slow walk, and many believe it is the hardest ascent in the British Isles.
Fun fact: Carnedd means cairn, while it is believed that the name Llywelyn comes from Prince Llywelyn, the last Prince of Wales, or perhaps his grandfather Llywelyn the Great.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 4. Glyder Fawr (Eryri National Park)
Glyder Fawr is the highest peak in the Glyderau range in Eryri. Standing at 1,000 m (3,280 ft), it is another impressive mountain within Eryri National Park.
It is the fifth-highest mountain in Wales and has several routes of varying difficulty leading to its summit. Climbers who reach the top are met with breathtaking views of the surrounding peaks and valleys.
This is because the Glyderau mountains are separated from surrounding mountain ranges by various valleys, making them stand out.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 5.Tryfan (Eryri National Park)
Also of the Glyderau range is a mountain called Tryfan. It stands at just over 917 m (3,008 ft) above sea level, making it one of the 14 highest peaks in Wales.
The triangular peak offers fantastic views from the top. The summit also features two pillars known as ‘Sion a Siân’ to locals or ‘Adam and Eve’ to non-Welsh speaking tourists.
Some braver climbers like to challenge themselves by jumping from one pillar to the other. Successful jumpers will gain the ‘Freedom of Tryfan’ whereas those who are unsuccessful are met with a likely painful landing – so leap at your own risk!
Fun fact: The name Tryfan is derived from ‘Tri-faen’ (three rocks) because from a distance, the mountain looks like a three-headed fin (a narrow, residual wall of hard sedimentary rock).

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 6. Cadair Idris (Eryri National Park)
Cadair Idris is the highest mountain in southern Eryri, standing at 893 m (2,929 ft) high. Located near the town of Dolgellau, its distinctive peak can be seen for miles around. So it’s no surprise this is one of the more popular mountains in Wales.
The climb is actually included in the Welsh Three Peaks Challenge alongside Wales’s most famous mountains, the Yr Wyddfa and Pen Y Fan.
The challenge is designed so that climbers and tourists can experience an intense but memorable 24-hour road trip across Wales, where they get to climb all three peaks in one round-trip!

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 7. Waun Fach (The Black Mountains)
Next in this Welsh mountains list, is a mountain called Waun Fach, situated in a mountain range called The Black Mountains. Waun Fach is the highest peak in the range at 811 m (2,660 ft) high.
The Black Mountains are located on the English border and from Waun Fach, climbers can see views over Abergavenny and Brecon from the top.
Fun fact: The mountain is well known for its curved summit.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 8. Fan Brycheiniog (Black Mountain)
Located within the boundaries of Brecon Beacons National Park is a very similarly named mountain range to the previously mentioned Black Mountains: the Black Mountain. Here you’ll find Fan Brycheiniog, the highest peak in the range at 802 m (2,631 ft) high.
Fun fact: At the foot of the mountain lies a lake named Llyn y Fan Fawr. Created as a result of glacial action, the lake is one of the largest glacial lakes in South Wales.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### **9. Plynlimon (Cambrian Mountains)**
Plynlimon is the highest mountain in the Cambrian mountain range, standing at 752 m (2,467 ft) high.
Located in Mid Wales, the Cambrian mountains are neighboured by the Brecon Beacons and stretch from Machynlleth to Llandovery.
Fun fact: Both the River Severn and the River Wye originate in the Cambrian Mountains.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 10. Foel Cwmcerwyn (Preseli Hills)
Foel Cwmcerwyn is the highest peak in the Preseli Hills and the smallest mountain (being under 600m it’s actually a hill) in this list, standing at 536 m (1,758 ft) high.
There are 15 other peaks located there. These include:
*   Carn Ingli – Standing at 347 m (1,338 ft) high, Carn Ingli is close to the coast and is clearly visible among the surrounding countryside. It’s a relatively easy climb, but it does have a pretty steep slope in some areas. The mountain is marked as a Site of Scientific Interest (SSSI).  
*   Foel Eryr – Standing at 404 m (1,325 ft) high, Foel Eryr is actually one of the easiest of the Preseli Hills to climb and the quickest. There you’ll find a Bronze Age burial cairn among other glimpses of rich history. The views from the top are also spectacular, and you may even spot some moorland birds!  
*   Foel Drygarn – 360 m (1,190 ft) high. A fascinating location with lots of rich history. It was once an Iron Age hillfort as well as a Bronze Age burial cairn! Don’t forget that Drygarn translates to three cairns.  
*   Foel Feddau - 467 m (1,532 ft) high. At the summit of Foel Feddau you’ll find a damaged cairn.  
*   Frenni Fach - 301 m (988 ft) high. You will find a barrow at the summit of Frenni Fach. It formerly served as a Parish boundary marker.  
*   Frenni Fawr - 395 m (1,296 ft) high. Frenni Fawr holds an Iron Age Hill Fort and Bronze Age cairns.
As you can tell the Preseli Hills are of great historical interest. So you can enjoy a good walk and learn a thing or two while you’re at it.
The Preseli Hills can be found within the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park in Pembrokeshire, South West Wales.

## What’s the difference between Welsh hills and mountains?
Ever wondered how to tell the difference between a Welsh hill and a Welsh mountain? Well, unfortunately, it isn’t actually that straightforward.
Typically, people think of a mountain as a steep, sloping area of land that features sharp edges and a high point known as a summit or a peak.
Let’s take a look at what qualifies as a mountain according to the dictionary:
_“a raised part of the earth's surface, much larger than a hill, the top of which might be covered in snow”_
So what does ‘larger than a hill’ really mean, and when does a hill become a mountain? There is some confusion surrounding this and there is no real concrete answer, but many geologists argue that anything above 300 m (1,000 ft) should be classified as a mountain. However, the UK government considers anything above 610 m (2,000 ft) to be the threshold.

## List of Welsh hills
Let’s take a look at some of the incredible Welsh hills, and where to find them. While they are much smaller than some of the mountains listed above, all of these Welsh hills are well worth the trip! They're perfect for walkers who are looking for destinations that won't take as much of a toll on their bodies while still enabling them to witness some amazing views from the top!

# What do we do - P600 Mountaineering
## Adventures
### Guided walks across the UK.
At P600 Mountaineering, we specialise in guided walks across some of the UK’s most iconic and inspiring landscapes—including **Scotland**, **Eryri (Snowdonia)**, **Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons)**, and the **Lake District.**
In North Wales, we run regular day hikes to popular peaks such as **Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)**, **Tryfan**, and **Cadair Idris** in Eryri, as well as **Pen y Fan** in Bannau Brycheiniog for those seeking adventure in South Wales. But we don’t just stick to the well-trodden path —we love exploring quieter corners like the **Carneddau**, **Rhinogs**, and **Moelwyns**, offering a more peaceful and authentic Welsh mountain experience.
The **Lake District Fells**, made famous by Alfred Wainwright, are among our favourite places to roam. Whether you're aiming to summit **Scafell Pike** or discover lesser-known fell tops away from the crowds, we’ll help you experience the Lakes in a more personal and rewarding way.
And then there’s **Scotland**—the heart of UK mountaineering. From standing atop **Ben Nevis,** the UK’s highest peak, to soaking in the vast views from **Ben Macdui** in the Cairngorms, the Highlands and Islands offer endless opportunities for adventure. With **282 Munros**, **222 Corbetts**, and **231 Grahams**to choose from, we’re truly spoiled for choice—and we’d love to help you explore them.

# What do we do - P600 Mountaineering
## Training
### Navigation Skills Training
Whether you're just starting out or looking to sharpen your skills, we offer navigation training to suit every level. From a gentle introduction to map reading and compass use, through to achieving your NNAS Silver Award, we’re here to help you grow in confidence and capability.
Our courses are practical, supportive, and designed to empower you to explore independently. They're ideal for complete beginners as well as experienced hillwalkers looking to refine their technique with more advanced navigation strategies.
If you're a trainee Mountain Leader preparing for assessment, I’d be happy to join you for a tailored skills day—focusing on the areas you want to develop most. Whether it’s micro-navigation, relocation strategies, or rope work, we’ll work together to help you feel confident and assessment-ready.
Let us help you build the skills to explore with confidence, wherever your adventures take you.

# What do we do - P600 Mountaineering
## Bespoke
### Bespoke Events for Private, Charity or Corporate Groups
Planning a private, charity, or corporate adventure? We’d love to help bring your vision to life.
If you have a group of two or more and want to explore the wild places of the UK, we can create a fully tailored experience to match your goals—whether you're after a quiet day in nature, a team-building challenge, or something completely unique. ## How many mountains are there in Wales?
Wales is well-known for its mountainous terrain. But just how many mountains are there in Wales altogether? Although Wales is a small country covering just over 8,000 square miles, it’s famous for its numerous beautiful mountains – many of which were created during the last Ice Age approximately 12,000 years ago.
There are several mountain ranges here, spread across 13 regions. Within these ranges, there are a grand total of 136 mountains over 600 m (2,000 ft) high, and many more which don’t reach those lofty heights! Some of Wales’ most beloved hills are the Garn Boduan, the Mynydd Llangyndeyrn, Mynydd Dinas, Bryn Arw, and Mynydd Anelog.
**Fun fact:** The definition of a mountain is a rise which is 600m or, 2000ft above sea level. Mountains of this height are also known as ‘Hewitts’ in the United Kingdom. There are 525 Hewitts altogether in the UK.

## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
The highest mountain in Wales is Snowdon, Yr Wyddfa in Welsh, and it is located in the Eryri National Park. It stands at 1085 m (3,559 ft) high. The peak features at number one on the list of 15 Welsh mountains called the Welsh 3,000s (mountains over 914 m (3,000 ft).
All 15 of Wales’ highest mountains are part of the Eryri National Park region, but there are other mountainous regions that are home to some of the most fantastic mountains in Wales.
Check out the Welsh mountains list below to find out more about Wales’ mountainous regions.
texts.7:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 1. Snowdon, or Yr Wyddfa (Eryri National Park)
‘Yr Wyddfa’ is Wales’ highest mountain, standing at an incredible 1085 m (3559 ft) high! The peak is also one of Wales’ most famous landmarks, located in Eryri National Park, North Wales.
There are five main ranges within the National Park, these include the Snowdon massif itself as well the following:
*   Glyderau

*   Carneddau

*   Moelwynion

*   Moel Hebog
Wales’ highest mountains can be found within the Snowdon massif, Glyderau and Carneddau. Other ranges situated within the wider National Park are the Rhinogydd and the Cadair Idris and Aran Fawddwy ranges.
‘Yr Wyddfa’ was formed over millions of years, following numerous volcanic eruptions and glaciers forming and melting. The mountain is home to a rare flower called The Snowdon Lily, thought to have been around since the end of the Ice Age! It is the only known location in the UK that this flower has been spotted.
Hikers can choose from six eight-mile trails, of mixed difficulty, to reach the summit. However, the location is so popular, there is a train that can take visitors to the top where they will also find a visitor centre called Hafod Eryri.
The first recorded successful climb to the top of the mountain was by a man named Thomas Johnson in 1639.
Fun fact: ‘Yr Wyddfa’ is so high, that you can see across the sea to Ireland when standing at the summit!
texts.8:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 2. Pen y Fan (Brecon Beacons)
Another incredibly popular peak in Wales is Pen y Fan (meaning ‘Top of the Beacons’ in English), situated in the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park. Standing at 886 m (2,906 ft) high, it is the highest mountain in South Wales.
In fact, the landmark is so popular among hikers and tourists that the mountain and surrounding area are owned and maintained by the National Trust. The organisation works to prevent erosion caused by walkers due to its popularity.
The mountain is also used in military training exercises as part of the selection process for the UK’s Special Forces.
The Brecon Beacons are home to some of the most loved mountains in Britain. There are six main peaks:
*   Pen y Fan – 886 m (2,906 ft)  
*   Corn Du – 873 m (2,864 ft)  
*   Cribyn – 795 m (2,608 ft)  
*   Waun Rydd – 769 m (2,522 ft)  
*   Bwlch y Ddwyallt – 754 m (2,473 ft)  
*   Fan y Bîg – 719 m (2,358 ft)
Fun fact: Pen y Fan and Corn Du, also known as the twin summits, were once referred to as Cadair Arthur or 'Arthur's Seat' after the Welsh legend, King Arthur.
texts.9:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 3. Carnedd Llywelyn (Eryri National Park)
Standing at 1064 m (3,490 ft), Carnedd Llywelyn is the highest point of the Carneddau range in Eryri.
You’ll find the summit located between two other mountains, Carnedd Dafydd and Foel Grach as well as cliffs for climbing including Craig yr Ysfa and the ‘Black Ladders’ of Ysgolion Duon.
Climbing Carnedd Llewelyn requires a long, slow walk, and many believe it is the hardest ascent in the British Isles.
Fun fact: Carnedd means cairn, while it is believed that the name Llywelyn comes from Prince Llywelyn, the last Prince of Wales, or perhaps his grandfather Llywelyn the Great.
texts.10:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 4. Glyder Fawr (Eryri National Park)
Glyder Fawr is the highest peak in the Glyderau range in Eryri. Standing at 1,000 m (3,280 ft), it is another impressive mountain within Eryri National Park.
It is the fifth-highest mountain in Wales and has several routes of varying difficulty leading to its summit. Climbers who reach the top are met with breathtaking views of the surrounding peaks and valleys.
This is because the Glyderau mountains are separated from surrounding mountain ranges by various valleys, making them stand out.
texts.11:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 5.Tryfan (Eryri National Park)
Also of the Glyderau range is a mountain called Tryfan. It stands at just over 917 m (3,008 ft) above sea level, making it one of the 14 highest peaks in Wales.
The triangular peak offers fantastic views from the top. The summit also features two pillars known as ‘Sion a Siân’ to locals or ‘Adam and Eve’ to non-Welsh speaking tourists.
Some braver climbers like to challenge themselves by jumping from one pillar to the other. Successful jumpers will gain the ‘Freedom of Tryfan’ whereas those who are unsuccessful are met with a likely painful landing – so leap at your own risk!
Fun fact: The name Tryfan is derived from ‘Tri-faen’ (three rocks) because from a distance, the mountain looks like a three-headed fin (a narrow, residual wall of hard sedimentary rock).
texts.12:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 6. Cadair Idris (Eryri National Park)
Cadair Idris is the highest mountain in southern Eryri, standing at 893 m (2,929 ft) high. Located near the town of Dolgellau, its distinctive peak can be seen for miles around. So it’s no surprise this is one of the more popular mountains in Wales.
The climb is actually included in the Welsh Three Peaks Challenge alongside Wales’s most famous mountains, the Yr Wyddfa and Pen Y Fan.
The challenge is designed so that climbers and tourists can experience an intense but memorable 24-hour road trip across Wales, where they get to climb all three peaks in one round-trip!
texts.13:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 7. Waun Fach (The Black Mountains)
Next in this Welsh mountains list, is a mountain called Waun Fach, situated in a mountain range called The Black Mountains. Waun Fach is the highest peak in the range at 811 m (2,660 ft) high.
The Black Mountains are located on the English border and from Waun Fach, climbers can see views over Abergavenny and Brecon from the top.
Fun fact: The mountain is well known for its curved summit.
texts.14:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 8. Fan Brycheiniog (Black Mountain)
Located within the boundaries of Brecon Beacons National Park is a very similarly named mountain range to the previously mentioned Black Mountains: the Black Mountain. Here you’ll find Fan Brycheiniog, the highest peak in the range at 802 m (2,631 ft) high.
Fun fact: At the foot of the mountain lies a lake named Llyn y Fan Fawr. Created as a result of glacial action, the lake is one of the largest glacial lakes in South Wales.
texts.15:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### **9. Plynlimon (Cambrian Mountains)**
Plynlimon is the highest mountain in the Cambrian mountain range, standing at 752 m (2,467 ft) high.
Located in Mid Wales, the Cambrian mountains are neighboured by the Brecon Beacons and stretch from Machynlleth to Llandovery.
Fun fact: Both the River Severn and the River Wye originate in the Cambrian Mountains.
texts.16:
## What is the highest mountain in Wales?
### 10. Foel Cwmcerwyn (Preseli Hills)
Foel Cwmcerwyn is the highest peak in the Preseli Hills and the smallest mountain (being under 600m it’s actually a hill) in this list, standing at 536 m (1,758 ft) high.
There are 15 other peaks located there. These include:
*   Carn Ingli – Standing at 347 m (1,338 ft) high, Carn Ingli is close to the coast and is clearly visible among the surrounding countryside. It’s a relatively easy climb, but it does have a pretty steep slope in some areas. The mountain is marked as a Site of Scientific Interest (SSSI).  
*   Foel Eryr – Standing at 404 m (1,325 ft) high, Foel Eryr is actually one of the easiest of the Preseli Hills to climb and the quickest. There you’ll find a Bronze Age burial cairn among other glimpses of rich history. The views from the top are also spectacular, and you may even spot some moorland birds!  
*   Foel Drygarn – 360 m (1,190 ft) high. A fascinating location with lots of rich history. It was once an Iron Age hillfort as well as a Bronze Age burial cairn! Don’t forget that Drygarn translates to three cairns.  
*   Foel Feddau - 467 m (1,532 ft) high. At the summit of Foel Feddau you’ll find a damaged cairn.  
*   Frenni Fach - 301 m (988 ft) high. You will find a barrow at the summit of Frenni Fach. It formerly served as a Parish boundary marker.  
*   Frenni Fawr - 395 m (1,296 ft) high. Frenni Fawr holds an Iron Age Hill Fort and Bronze Age cairns.
As you can tell the Preseli Hills are of great historical interest. So you can enjoy a good walk and learn a thing or two while you’re at it.
The Preseli Hills can be found within the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park in Pembrokeshire, South West Wales.
texts.17:
## What’s the difference between Welsh hills and mountains?
Ever wondered how to tell the difference between a Welsh hill and a Welsh mountain? Well, unfortunately, it isn’t actually that straightforward.
Typically, people think of a mountain as a steep, sloping area of land that features sharp edges and a high point known as a summit or a peak.
Let’s take a look at what qualifies as a mountain according to the dictionary:
_“a raised part of the earth's surface, much larger than a hill, the top of which might be covered in snow”_
So what does ‘larger than a hill’ really mean, and when does a hill become a mountain? There is some confusion surrounding this and there is no real concrete answer, but many geologists argue that anything above 300 m (1,000 ft) should be classified as a mountain. However, the UK government considers anything above 610 m (2,000 ft) to be the threshold.

Mountains of Wales
The Welsh mountains that make our landscapes so distinctive were carved out in the Ice Age, some 10,000 years ago. They’re our defence and our lifeline, a challenge and an inspiration. Their peaks, slopes and views are endlessly exciting to explore.
texts.1:
## Eryri
Rocky, rough and tough – that's how we like our mountains. Don’t think that just because you can take a train to the top,Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon)isn't a proper peak. In fact,Eryri (Snowdonia) National Parkis a mountain and adventure capital that's up there with the classic Alpine destinations.
Each of the six official eight-mile routes to the highest mountain in Wales(1085m) offer sensational hiking and incredible views. In Eryri's nine ranges, there are 15 peaks over 900m high, including Yr Wyddfa itself. You may have heard of some of the others.Tryfan (918m) is a famous landmark:a triangular peak offering some of the best scrambling – and views – in Britain. Meanwhile, Cader Idris is 893m high and rears up from the shores of the beautiful Mawddach Estuary.
texts.2:
## Cambrian Mountains
The Cambrian Mountains is a name that describes the sparsely-populated landscape from Foel Fadian (563m) near Penfforddlas and Pumlumon Fawr (752m) near Ponterwyd in the north, all the way south through the Elenydd and the Elan Valley to Mynydd Mallaen (462m) near Llanymddyfri (Llandovery).At its southernmost tip you’ll discover Mynydd Llanfihangel-rhos-y-corn (356m) near Brechfa Forest. The Cambrian Mountains span the three counties of Powys, Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire.
Located between Eryri and the Bannau Brycheiniog (the Brecon Beacons), the Cambrian Mountains include cairned summits, open moorland and lush valleys. They are home to the sources of the rivers Wye and the Severn and the peaceful Elan Valley reservoirs.
By day walk some local and National Trails, journey on your mountain bike or horse and even paraglide from quiet nearby peaks. By night you will discover some of the darkest skies in Europe by visiting the many Dark Sky Discovery Sites on the Cambrian Mountains Astro Trail.
texts.3:
## Black Mountain Range, the Black Mountains, Fforest Fawr, and the Bannau Brycheiniog
The Black Mountain Range and the Black Mountains aren’t one and the same, although they are both found within the grassy expanses of theBannau Brycheiniog National Park. The Black Mountain Range, sometimes just called Black Mountain, is to the west, north of Swansea. It’s one of Wales’ most wild and remote corners with impressive, glacier-carved escarpments and isolated lakes, several miles from the nearest road. Its highest peak is Fan Brycheiniog (802m).
The Black Mountains are to the east, on the border with England. Y Fenni (Abergavenny), Y Gelli Gandryll (Hay-on-Wye), Llangorse, and the Monmouthshire & Brecon Canal stand at their feet, and their highest point is the Waun Fach plateau (811m). Confusingly enough, this range is also home to a peak called Black Mountain.
To the southwest isFforest Fawr(Great Forest), an upland area of remarkable limestone cliffs and caves. It was the the first Geopark in Wales.
Dominating the centre of the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park are the Bannau Brycheiniog, whose most celebrated peaks, Pen y Fan (886m) and Cribyn (795m), are the highest in southern Britain. The Bannau Brycheiniog are popular, with plenty of footpaths and bridleways. But they’re quieter than Eryri. Head off on foot and at times it can feel as if you have an entire mountainside to yourself.

This page includes a map of the mountains of Britain and Ireland which qualify as 'P600 Mountains'. You may use it for reference, or in the completion of your quest to climb all the P600 mountains in Britain and Ireland.
A P600 is defined as a mountain with a topographic prominence above 600 metres. By definition, P600s have a height above 600 metres (1,969 feet), the qualified requirement to be called a "mountain" in the British Isles.
Essentially, the mountains in the P600 list should all be clearly identifiable, as each has a standalone mass rising to 600 metres or over.
**Using the Map:**
By clicking on any mountain on the map, a pop-out list shows details on the particular mountain's height and prominence, in both metres and feet. _Each rises 600m or more from its surroundings; there are 119 of them; and they're scattered all over Britain and Ireland, from Kerry to Scotland's far north. Meet the P600s, and the man who bagged them all in 93 days._
* * *
**I first came across the P600s in 2018, while perusing hill-bagging.co.uk like any obsessive peak bagger. These peaks immediately captivated me for two reasons. Firstly, they encompassed all of the British Isles, rather than a specific country. Secondly, their sole criteria, a topographic prominence of 600m (1,968.5ft), distinguished them from most other mountain categories. When I found out there were only 10 known completers, but it was unclear what the fastest known time (FKT) was, I felt that this was a challenge to test myself against. I plotted an itinerary, complete with routes, based on the intention of ascending the 119 P600s as one continuous round.**
Schiehallion summit selfie  
© Simon Tull
Since the original draft, the fundamentals of the challenge never changed:
*   I would follow direct out and back routes to each P600, so I would not complete many of their "classic" routes.  
*   Sometimes the most direct route would entail ascending other categorised peaks along the way, but I would not go out of my way to do so.  
*   I would ascend 2 P600s most days ("double peak days").
I created four distinct phases: starting with the 25 P600s in Ireland, my focus would then turn to the 16 P600s scattered across the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland. Afterwards, I would begin what I felt was the real challenge, the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland. The final stretch would take in the last 12 P600s spread across England, the Isle of Man and Wales.
> Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute

The itinerary itself was 92 days with almost every hiking day being a double peak day. The only exceptions were a triple peak day during Phase One, Ireland, and then single peak days for both Ben Alder and Snowdon, the latter being my final P600. I had designed the itinerary to be flexible as I was aware double peak days for most of Phase Three, the Scottish mainland, were not feasible as the routes during this stage were generally longer and with far more ascent required. Until I knew what I was capable of and what my daily limits for mileage and ascent should be, I would keep Phase Three as plotted, reasoning that it would be easier to spread out the P600s once the challenge was underway.
I was confident my schedules for Phases One, Two and Four were accurate, but given the above, my gut feeling was that Phase Three would take between 8-12 weeks, meaning the challenge could actually take up to 121 days.
I encountered a fellow enthusiast, Liam Chase, in mid-2019 whilst he was in the midst of his own bid to set the FKT for the P600s. I even joined him for a few routes. Liam was aware that we had the same goal, though our methods differed as he was completing his challenge on the weekends around his job. He would become the 15th person known to have scaled the P600s and, more importantly, the first to achieve this in a calendar year in 313 days.
My ambition persisted and every couple of years I would refine the itinerary when it felt like things were coming together to finally undertake this endeavour. After a couple of false starts, the stars began to align in late 2024.
Whilst I would ascend the P600s, Siobhan, my partner, would support me throughout the entirety of the challenge, most significantly by driving, as I cannot do this myself. I could have embarked on a self-powered feat by cycling between the P600s, but that would have at least doubled how long the challenge would last, if not more.
> I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham

The duration was also crucial for another reason: the challenge would be entirely self-funded. I had saved enough funds to cover our monthly commitments at home as well as our day-to-day spending during the challenge, based on the expectation that it could take up to 121 days to complete. Our continued employment was another consideration, as we envisioned this would be easier to secure if the challenge only took up to 121 days. After approaching our employers, I was granted a sabbatical but, sadly, Siobhan would have to leave her career of 10 years (an effective way to motivate me to finish it early!).
We originally intended to complete the challenge using a tent box mounted on our car. After testing this setup in early April, we thankfully had a reality check as to how optimistic we were being. Although ideal for short trips, the tent box was clearly not going to work for up to 17 weeks. We bought a converted van in mid-April, a fortnight before the challenge started. Alongside the van, we booked the occasional hotel whenever we needed some comfort, though in practice I was the one who needed this most.
In some respects, Phases One and Two would serve as a test bed, allowing us to adjust to and then fine tune what van life resembled to us, all the while figuring out how accurate our preconceptions about day-to-day life during the challenge actually were. In a similar vein, I had long considered Phases One and Two to be the final stage of my training ahead of what I strongly felt was the "real" challenge, Phase Three.
A couple of days before the challenge commenced, we sailed to Ireland. There was no going back. I just hoped that my middle-aged fitness and male grade navigation were enough to get me through!
> Despite hail and snow I smiled; there was nowhere else I'd rather be

#### Phase One – Ireland
_Friday 25th April to Thursday 8th May_
Journeying anti-clockwise around Ireland, I planned to ascend the 25 P600s located there in three blocks of four hiking days with a rest day wedged in between. It was wet and windy on Lugnaquilla, a fine start to the challenge and hopefully not a precedent. The weather was mixed for a few days until a four-week dry spell ensued that would last until late May. Barrclashcame would cement itself as the toughest ascent of the challenge, the measure against which future arduous ascents were compared. Croaghaun was the P600 that I was most looking forward to. Once I was near the summit of Ireland's highest sea cliff, the views I had longed to witness simply plummeted down into the ocean.
Phase One ended when we boarded the overnight ferry at Belfast, arriving in Liverpool the next morning. We had a 28-hour layover at home in Penrith before we needed to leave to catch another ferry. The short turnaround taught us a great deal about managing future returns, mainly that it was barely enough time to clean the van and our laundry!

#### Phase Two – Scotland (Islands and Peninsulas)
_Sunday 11th to Wednesday 21st May_
Phase Two was undoubtedly the most time-sensitive stage of the challenge, an 11-day odyssey of the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland, amidst which we needed to catch 16 ferries. The 16 P600s I would pursue were spread over two blocks of five hiking days with a single rest day in the middle.
We first hopped between Arran, Jura, Mull and the Ardgour peninsula. Despite years of refining my routes, Creach Bheinn was the first P600 where I identified a better route halfway through my own. Although this was bound to happen, I stuck to my route. The next day, I had my first setback. I was due to summit Garbh Bheinn and then Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill, but the former was a tough route. I moved Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill to the following day when I was due to be on the Knoydart peninsula, meaning Ladhar Bheinn would need to be rescheduled for later, an easy prospect as Phase Three would bring us near to Mallaig again. We finished up on Rùm, Skye, South Uist and Harris. Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute. It was slow progress heading up this immense scree gully, the hard work only becoming worthwhile by the amount of fun I had sailing back down in just 20 mins! I reached the 1/3 milestone on day 27 with Clisham, my 40th P600, before returning to the mainland.
The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh  
© Simon Tull

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
_Friday 23rd May to Sunday 20th July_
Phase Three was split into a trio of subsections that were intended to make the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland more manageable. These subsections lasted 4.5 days, five weeks and 13 days respectively, with a break of three days at home in between each.
The first subsection was a loop around the far north of Scotland, just as the four-week dry spell came to an end. Things soon unravelled. After I descended from Canisp, I didn't feel strong enough to continue onto Ben More Assynt the same day, so I ended up ascending the latter the next day. When we returned to Penrith a few days later, I realised I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham and this had persisted ever since. In hindsight, rescheduling Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill during Phase Two was the first sign that I was tiring. Siobhan and I adjusted the portion sizes for all of my meals and this seemed to do the trick.
Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes  
© Simon Tull
As mentioned earlier, a significant proportion of Phase Three should have been plotted as single peak days. Now that I knew my capabilities, I imposed daily limits of 18 miles and/or 7,500ft of ascent as I reworked the itinerary for the five-week subsection. Over half of my upcoming hiking days became single peak days.

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Phase Three resumed as we proceeded to work down the Scottish mainland. I endured the harshest conditions that I have ever been exposed to during my back-to-back ascents of An Teallach: Bidein a' Ghlas Thuill and Sgùrr Mòr in the Fannichs. Despite having hail and snow driven into me by gale-force winds between 50-60mph, I responded as I would do every other time I was faced with hardship during the challenge, by smiling and laughing to myself, for there was nowhere else I'd rather be. After scaling Sgorr Ruadh, my 60th P600 and the halfway milestone on day 45, I surprised Siobhan when we checked into the Cluanie Inn as a halfway treat for a couple of nights around a rest day. By now, I had realised that I could feasibly complete the challenge in around 100 days by early August.
Suitably rested, we meandered into some remote glens west of Loch Ness before venturing to the far end of Loch Arkaig. This is when my second setback occurred. I was supposed to ascend both Sgùrr na Cìche and Càrn Mòr as part of a mammoth route as they stand on opposite ends of Glen Dessarry (these are the only two P600s which can be reasonably combined). I summited the former and wandered to the base of the steep grassy slope that started the long traverse to Càrn Mòr. Realising that completing my route would take longer than anticipated and having no way of updating Siobhan as I was out of signal, the correct course was to leave Càrn Mòr for another time.

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Whilst resting near Fort William, I reflected on the times when the isolation of hiking by myself on a tight schedule and in poor weather had begun to gnaw at me. I actually enjoy hiking in poor weather, so it was a telling sign as to how gruelling the conditions were. More so than any other point, I keenly felt the slow progress owing to the frequent single peak days, which, alongside the weather, made this stage of the challenge the least enjoyable. In spite of this, I never turned back. I have no profound answer as to how I managed to stay motivated. My overriding impulse was that the challenge was what I had always wanted, and it was not meant to be easy.
It was fitting that Ladhar Bheinn was the first P600 I scaled after skipping Càrn Mòr. The following week saw me work my way back towards Fort William. On Gulvain, I met Arran Evison, who had recently started his own challenge to be the youngest person to complete the Munros on a mountain bike. It was a timely encounter given my recent introspection and afterwards, I felt a renewed conviction about myself. We then headed to the Cairngorms, where my uncle joined me for Ben Macdui, the first time I had been accompanied on a hike during the challenge. On day 68, I reached my 80th P600, Beinn a' Ghlò: Càrn nan Gabhar, the 2/3 milestone.
The five-week subsection ended with Ben Alder, the most intimidating P600, given that a 26-mile route is required to reach the summit. Of course, I headed up in heavy rain! Crossing the Allt a'Bhealaich Bheithe was fraught as the river was heavily in spate. There were some rocks to hop over on my way out, but on my return, I simply waded through the waist-deep water. After five weeks away, I just wanted to get home.
Descending from Beinn an Lochain  
© Simon Tull

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Upon deciding that Saturday 26th July would be the final day of the challenge, I adjusted the rest of the itinerary. There were 34 P600s left, so it would be a push to ascend these in 19 days, but doing so would mean the challenge would have taken me 93 days, an achievement that originally I did not believe was possible.
The remaining 22 P600s in Phase Three were split between two blocks of six hiking days separated by a rest day. Càrn Mòr was one of the first P600s I ascended after returning to Scotland for the last time. A heatwave then settled in as I marched up Beinn a' Chreachain, during which I became the proud owner of around 30 swollen horsefly bites. Our final two days in Scotland each had a yellow weather warning forecast, one for heavy rain on Saturday and one for thunderstorms on Sunday. Neither materialised and despite the threat looming overhead, it was eerily calm as I stood atop Broad Law, my 82nd and final P600 in Scotland, exactly 10 weeks after summiting the first, Goat Fell.
In the following days, I had this feeling that the challenge actually ended on Broad Law. I can only put this down to two things. Up until the end of Phase Three, Siobhan and I had existed in an intense and tightly scheduled environment and although there were still 12 P600s left, Phase Four would be considerably more relaxed than what came before. Additionally, as I had strongly felt that the Scottish mainland was the real challenge for so long, in some ways, Phase Three had become "the" challenge.
Longside Edge from Skiddaw at golden hour  
© Simon Tull

#### Phase Four – England, the Isle of Man and Wales
_Monday 21st to Saturday 26th July_
I was supposed to rest on the Monday before diving into Phase Four, the final stretch across the 12 P600s in England, the Isle of Man and Wales. Instead, I brought Skiddaw forward to make the Tuesday less crammed, meaning that I would finish the challenge on a 12-day stint as my last rest day had been on Monday 14th July.
I was joined on Scafell Pike and Cross Fell by Alex Staniforth, fresh from his own challenge in which he set a new FKT of 43 days for the Nuttalls. Having scaled the P600s in England, we then made fleeting visits to the Isle of Man and the Brecon Beacons. It was poignant that Wales was the last country we visited as this is where my love of hillwalking was first nurtured. The challenge concluded with a pair of triple peak days in Snowdonia, the first of which began with Aran Fawddwy, the only P600 which had the distinction of me failing to ascend it (twice!) before. After a brisk ascent of Glyder Fawr, we met my family at the Snowdon Mountain Railway station in Llanberis and waited for some others to arrive.
I was humbled by everyone who chose to be there for Snowdon, my final P600. We started up the Llanberis Path and met Siobhan and my family who had taken the train. Holding Siobhan's hand, I took a moment to reflect before touching the trig point that crowns Snowdon. Following a swift descent to Llanberis, I stopped my watch.
The challenge was over.
Big team on Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa, the final P600  
© Simon Tull

#### Everyone loves fun facts, so here's a few about the challenge:
*   It took 93 days to complete (including 20 rest days)  
*   I hiked 923.1 miles / the equivalent of 35.2 marathons  
*   I ascended 359,154ft / the equivalent of 12.4 Mount Everests  
*   I am the 16th person known to have ascended the P600s  
*   I am only the second person known to have ascended the P600s in a single calendar year (the other is Liam Chase)  
*   I am the first person to complete the P600s in the six years since Liam  
*   I had only ascended 19 P600s before the challenge  
*   Besides setting a new FKT, I smashed Liam's record by 220 days. We're still friends!
It was a privilege to raise funds for both Mind Over Mountains and Every Life Matters. I am grateful for their support in raising awareness of the challenge that I was taking on to support them.
I doubt that I will directly inspire the next person who vies to set a quicker FKT for the P600s, but I hope they ask me to be there on their last peak to shake their hand when they do. Records are meant to be broken, so I am excited for when I am surpassed.
As for what's next, setting a new FKT for the P600s was very much a once in a lifetime feat. I intend to reascend the P600s during my lifetime and complete their classic routes. Maybe I'll be the first person to complete a second round...?

This page includes a map of the mountains of Britain and Ireland which qualify as 'P600 Mountains'. You may use it for reference, or in the completion of your quest to climb all the P600 mountains in Britain and Ireland.
A P600 is defined as a mountain with a topographic prominence above 600 metres. By definition, P600s have a height above 600 metres (1,969 feet), the qualified requirement to be called a "mountain" in the British Isles.
Essentially, the mountains in the P600 list should all be clearly identifiable, as each has a standalone mass rising to 600 metres or over.
**Using the Map:**
By clicking on any mountain on the map, a pop-out list shows details on the particular mountain's height and prominence, in both metres and feet. Grid references, latitude, and longitude are also detailed. Additionally, a link leads you to the Wikipedia page for each individual mountain within the group.

_Each rises 600m or more from its surroundings; there are 119 of them; and they're scattered all over Britain and Ireland, from Kerry to Scotland's far north. Meet the P600s, and the man who bagged them all in 93 days._
* * *
**I first came across the P600s in 2018, while perusing hill-bagging.co.uk like any obsessive peak bagger. These peaks immediately captivated me for two reasons. Firstly, they encompassed all of the British Isles, rather than a specific country. Secondly, their sole criteria, a topographic prominence of 600m (1,968.5ft), distinguished them from most other mountain categories. When I found out there were only 10 known completers, but it was unclear what the fastest known time (FKT) was, I felt that this was a challenge to test myself against. I plotted an itinerary, complete with routes, based on the intention of ascending the 119 P600s as one continuous round.**
Schiehallion summit selfie  
© Simon Tull
Since the original draft, the fundamentals of the challenge never changed:
*   I would follow direct out and back routes to each P600, so I would not complete many of their "classic" routes.  
*   Sometimes the most direct route would entail ascending other categorised peaks along the way, but I would not go out of my way to do so.  
*   I would ascend 2 P600s most days ("double peak days").
I created four distinct phases: starting with the 25 P600s in Ireland, my focus would then turn to the 16 P600s scattered across the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland. Afterwards, I would begin what I felt was the real challenge, the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland. The final stretch would take in the last 12 P600s spread across England, the Isle of Man and Wales.
> Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute

The itinerary itself was 92 days with almost every hiking day being a double peak day. The only exceptions were a triple peak day during Phase One, Ireland, and then single peak days for both Ben Alder and Snowdon, the latter being my final P600. I had designed the itinerary to be flexible as I was aware double peak days for most of Phase Three, the Scottish mainland, were not feasible as the routes during this stage were generally longer and with far more ascent required. Until I knew what I was capable of and what my daily limits for mileage and ascent should be, I would keep Phase Three as plotted, reasoning that it would be easier to spread out the P600s once the challenge was underway.
I was confident my schedules for Phases One, Two and Four were accurate, but given the above, my gut feeling was that Phase Three would take between 8-12 weeks, meaning the challenge could actually take up to 121 days.
I encountered a fellow enthusiast, Liam Chase, in mid-2019 whilst he was in the midst of his own bid to set the FKT for the P600s. I even joined him for a few routes. Liam was aware that we had the same goal, though our methods differed as he was completing his challenge on the weekends around his job. He would become the 15th person known to have scaled the P600s and, more importantly, the first to achieve this in a calendar year in 313 days.
My ambition persisted and every couple of years I would refine the itinerary when it felt like things were coming together to finally undertake this endeavour. After a couple of false starts, the stars began to align in late 2024.
Whilst I would ascend the P600s, Siobhan, my partner, would support me throughout the entirety of the challenge, most significantly by driving, as I cannot do this myself. I could have embarked on a self-powered feat by cycling between the P600s, but that would have at least doubled how long the challenge would last, if not more.
> I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham

The duration was also crucial for another reason: the challenge would be entirely self-funded. I had saved enough funds to cover our monthly commitments at home as well as our day-to-day spending during the challenge, based on the expectation that it could take up to 121 days to complete. Our continued employment was another consideration, as we envisioned this would be easier to secure if the challenge only took up to 121 days. After approaching our employers, I was granted a sabbatical but, sadly, Siobhan would have to leave her career of 10 years (an effective way to motivate me to finish it early!).
We originally intended to complete the challenge using a tent box mounted on our car. After testing this setup in early April, we thankfully had a reality check as to how optimistic we were being. Although ideal for short trips, the tent box was clearly not going to work for up to 17 weeks. We bought a converted van in mid-April, a fortnight before the challenge started. Alongside the van, we booked the occasional hotel whenever we needed some comfort, though in practice I was the one who needed this most.
In some respects, Phases One and Two would serve as a test bed, allowing us to adjust to and then fine tune what van life resembled to us, all the while figuring out how accurate our preconceptions about day-to-day life during the challenge actually were. In a similar vein, I had long considered Phases One and Two to be the final stage of my training ahead of what I strongly felt was the "real" challenge, Phase Three.
A couple of days before the challenge commenced, we sailed to Ireland. There was no going back. I just hoped that my middle-aged fitness and male grade navigation were enough to get me through!
> Despite hail and snow I smiled; there was nowhere else I'd rather be

#### Phase One – Ireland
_Friday 25th April to Thursday 8th May_
Journeying anti-clockwise around Ireland, I planned to ascend the 25 P600s located there in three blocks of four hiking days with a rest day wedged in between. It was wet and windy on Lugnaquilla, a fine start to the challenge and hopefully not a precedent. The weather was mixed for a few days until a four-week dry spell ensued that would last until late May. Barrclashcame would cement itself as the toughest ascent of the challenge, the measure against which future arduous ascents were compared. Croaghaun was the P600 that I was most looking forward to. Once I was near the summit of Ireland's highest sea cliff, the views I had longed to witness simply plummeted down into the ocean.
Phase One ended when we boarded the overnight ferry at Belfast, arriving in Liverpool the next morning. We had a 28-hour layover at home in Penrith before we needed to leave to catch another ferry. The short turnaround taught us a great deal about managing future returns, mainly that it was barely enough time to clean the van and our laundry!

#### Phase Two – Scotland (Islands and Peninsulas)
_Sunday 11th to Wednesday 21st May_
Phase Two was undoubtedly the most time-sensitive stage of the challenge, an 11-day odyssey of the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland, amidst which we needed to catch 16 ferries. The 16 P600s I would pursue were spread over two blocks of five hiking days with a single rest day in the middle.
We first hopped between Arran, Jura, Mull and the Ardgour peninsula. Despite years of refining my routes, Creach Bheinn was the first P600 where I identified a better route halfway through my own. Although this was bound to happen, I stuck to my route. The next day, I had my first setback. I was due to summit Garbh Bheinn and then Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill, but the former was a tough route. I moved Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill to the following day when I was due to be on the Knoydart peninsula, meaning Ladhar Bheinn would need to be rescheduled for later, an easy prospect as Phase Three would bring us near to Mallaig again. We finished up on Rùm, Skye, South Uist and Harris. Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute. It was slow progress heading up this immense scree gully, the hard work only becoming worthwhile by the amount of fun I had sailing back down in just 20 mins! I reached the 1/3 milestone on day 27 with Clisham, my 40th P600, before returning to the mainland.
The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh  
© Simon Tull

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
_Friday 23rd May to Sunday 20th July_
Phase Three was split into a trio of subsections that were intended to make the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland more manageable. These subsections lasted 4.5 days, five weeks and 13 days respectively, with a break of three days at home in between each.
The first subsection was a loop around the far north of Scotland, just as the four-week dry spell came to an end. Things soon unravelled. After I descended from Canisp, I didn't feel strong enough to continue onto Ben More Assynt the same day, so I ended up ascending the latter the next day. When we returned to Penrith a few days later, I realised I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham and this had persisted ever since. In hindsight, rescheduling Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill during Phase Two was the first sign that I was tiring. Siobhan and I adjusted the portion sizes for all of my meals and this seemed to do the trick.
Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes  
© Simon Tull
As mentioned earlier, a significant proportion of Phase Three should have been plotted as single peak days. Now that I knew my capabilities, I imposed daily limits of 18 miles and/or 7,500ft of ascent as I reworked the itinerary for the five-week subsection. Over half of my upcoming hiking days became single peak days.

Phase Three resumed as we proceeded to work down the Scottish mainland. I endured the harshest conditions that I have ever been exposed to during my back-to-back ascents of An Teallach: Bidein a' Ghlas Thuill and Sgùrr Mòr in the Fannichs. Despite having hail and snow driven into me by gale-force winds between 50-60mph, I responded as I would do every other time I was faced with hardship during the challenge, by smiling and laughing to myself, for there was nowhere else I'd rather be. After scaling Sgorr Ruadh, my 60th P600 and the halfway milestone on day 45, I surprised Siobhan when we checked into the Cluanie Inn as a halfway treat for a couple of nights around a rest day. By now, I had realised that I could feasibly complete the challenge in around 100 days by early August.
Suitably rested, we meandered into some remote glens west of Loch Ness before venturing to the far end of Loch Arkaig. This is when my second setback occurred. I was supposed to ascend both Sgùrr na Cìche and Càrn Mòr as part of a mammoth route as they stand on opposite ends of Glen Dessarry (these are the only two P600s which can be reasonably combined). I summited the former and wandered to the base of the steep grassy slope that started the long traverse to Càrn Mòr. Realising that completing my route would take longer than anticipated and having no way of updating Siobhan as I was out of signal, the correct course was to leave Càrn Mòr for another time.

#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Whilst resting near Fort William, I reflected on the times when the isolation of hiking by myself on a tight schedule and in poor weather had begun to gnaw at me. I actually enjoy hiking in poor weather, so it was a telling sign as to how gruelling the conditions were. More so than any other point, I keenly felt the slow progress owing to the frequent single peak days, which, alongside the weather, made this stage of the challenge the least enjoyable. In spite of this, I never turned back. I have no profound answer as to how I managed to stay motivated. My overriding impulse was that the challenge was what I had always wanted, and it was not meant to be easy.
It was fitting that Ladhar Bheinn was the first P600 I scaled after skipping Càrn Mòr. The following week saw me work my way back towards Fort William.
