_Each rises 600m or more from its surroundings; there are 119 of them; and they're scattered all over Britain and Ireland, from Kerry to Scotland's far north. Meet the P600s, and the man who bagged them all in 93 days._
* * *
**I first came across the P600s in 2018, while perusing hill-bagging.co.uk like any obsessive peak bagger. These peaks immediately captivated me for two reasons. Firstly, they encompassed all of the British Isles, rather than a specific country. Secondly, their sole criteria, a topographic prominence of 600m (1,968.5ft), distinguished them from most other mountain categories. When I found out there were only 10 known completers, but it was unclear what the fastest known time (FKT) was, I felt that this was a challenge to test myself against. I plotted an itinerary, complete with routes, based on the intention of ascending the 119 P600s as one continuous round.**
Schiehallion summit selfie  
© Simon Tull
Since the original draft, the fundamentals of the challenge never changed:
*   I would follow direct out and back routes to each P600, so I would not complete many of their "classic" routes.  
*   Sometimes the most direct route would entail ascending other categorised peaks along the way, but I would not go out of my way to do so.  
*   I would ascend 2 P600s most days ("double peak days").
I created four distinct phases: starting with the 25 P600s in Ireland, my focus would then turn to the 16 P600s scattered across the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland. Afterwards, I would begin what I felt was the real challenge, the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland. The final stretch would take in the last 12 P600s spread across England, the Isle of Man and Wales.
> Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute
texts.1:
The itinerary itself was 92 days with almost every hiking day being a double peak day. The only exceptions were a triple peak day during Phase One, Ireland, and then single peak days for both Ben Alder and Snowdon, the latter being my final P600. I had designed the itinerary to be flexible as I was aware double peak days for most of Phase Three, the Scottish mainland, were not feasible as the routes during this stage were generally longer and with far more ascent required. Until I knew what I was capable of and what my daily limits for mileage and ascent should be, I would keep Phase Three as plotted, reasoning that it would be easier to spread out the P600s once the challenge was underway.
I was confident my schedules for Phases One, Two and Four were accurate, but given the above, my gut feeling was that Phase Three would take between 8-12 weeks, meaning the challenge could actually take up to 121 days.
I encountered a fellow enthusiast, Liam Chase, in mid-2019 whilst he was in the midst of his own bid to set the FKT for the P600s. I even joined him for a few routes. Liam was aware that we had the same goal, though our methods differed as he was completing his challenge on the weekends around his job. He would become the 15th person known to have scaled the P600s and, more importantly, the first to achieve this in a calendar year in 313 days.
My ambition persisted and every couple of years I would refine the itinerary when it felt like things were coming together to finally undertake this endeavour. After a couple of false starts, the stars began to align in late 2024.
Whilst I would ascend the P600s, Siobhan, my partner, would support me throughout the entirety of the challenge, most significantly by driving, as I cannot do this myself. I could have embarked on a self-powered feat by cycling between the P600s, but that would have at least doubled how long the challenge would last, if not more.
> I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham
texts.2:
The duration was also crucial for another reason: the challenge would be entirely self-funded. I had saved enough funds to cover our monthly commitments at home as well as our day-to-day spending during the challenge, based on the expectation that it could take up to 121 days to complete. Our continued employment was another consideration, as we envisioned this would be easier to secure if the challenge only took up to 121 days. After approaching our employers, I was granted a sabbatical but, sadly, Siobhan would have to leave her career of 10 years (an effective way to motivate me to finish it early!).
We originally intended to complete the challenge using a tent box mounted on our car. After testing this setup in early April, we thankfully had a reality check as to how optimistic we were being. Although ideal for short trips, the tent box was clearly not going to work for up to 17 weeks. We bought a converted van in mid-April, a fortnight before the challenge started. Alongside the van, we booked the occasional hotel whenever we needed some comfort, though in practice I was the one who needed this most.
In some respects, Phases One and Two would serve as a test bed, allowing us to adjust to and then fine tune what van life resembled to us, all the while figuring out how accurate our preconceptions about day-to-day life during the challenge actually were. In a similar vein, I had long considered Phases One and Two to be the final stage of my training ahead of what I strongly felt was the "real" challenge, Phase Three.
A couple of days before the challenge commenced, we sailed to Ireland. There was no going back. I just hoped that my middle-aged fitness and male grade navigation were enough to get me through!
> Despite hail and snow I smiled; there was nowhere else I'd rather be
texts.3:
#### Phase One – Ireland
_Friday 25th April to Thursday 8th May_
Journeying anti-clockwise around Ireland, I planned to ascend the 25 P600s located there in three blocks of four hiking days with a rest day wedged in between. It was wet and windy on Lugnaquilla, a fine start to the challenge and hopefully not a precedent. The weather was mixed for a few days until a four-week dry spell ensued that would last until late May. Barrclashcame would cement itself as the toughest ascent of the challenge, the measure against which future arduous ascents were compared. Croaghaun was the P600 that I was most looking forward to. Once I was near the summit of Ireland's highest sea cliff, the views I had longed to witness simply plummeted down into the ocean.
Phase One ended when we boarded the overnight ferry at Belfast, arriving in Liverpool the next morning. We had a 28-hour layover at home in Penrith before we needed to leave to catch another ferry. The short turnaround taught us a great deal about managing future returns, mainly that it was barely enough time to clean the van and our laundry!
texts.4:
#### Phase Two – Scotland (Islands and Peninsulas)
_Sunday 11th to Wednesday 21st May_
Phase Two was undoubtedly the most time-sensitive stage of the challenge, an 11-day odyssey of the islands and peninsulas on the west coast of Scotland, amidst which we needed to catch 16 ferries. The 16 P600s I would pursue were spread over two blocks of five hiking days with a single rest day in the middle.
We first hopped between Arran, Jura, Mull and the Ardgour peninsula. Despite years of refining my routes, Creach Bheinn was the first P600 where I identified a better route halfway through my own. Although this was bound to happen, I stuck to my route. The next day, I had my first setback. I was due to summit Garbh Bheinn and then Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill, but the former was a tough route. I moved Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill to the following day when I was due to be on the Knoydart peninsula, meaning Ladhar Bheinn would need to be rescheduled for later, an easy prospect as Phase Three would bring us near to Mallaig again. We finished up on Rùm, Skye, South Uist and Harris. Sgùrr Alasdair was the P600 that I was most cautious about due to the infamous Great Stone Chute. It was slow progress heading up this immense scree gully, the hard work only becoming worthwhile by the amount of fun I had sailing back down in just 20 mins! I reached the 1/3 milestone on day 27 with Clisham, my 40th P600, before returning to the mainland.
The ferocious Aonach Eagach from the benign Sgòrr nam Fiannaidh  
© Simon Tull
texts.5:
#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
_Friday 23rd May to Sunday 20th July_
Phase Three was split into a trio of subsections that were intended to make the 66 P600s on the Scottish mainland more manageable. These subsections lasted 4.5 days, five weeks and 13 days respectively, with a break of three days at home in between each.
The first subsection was a loop around the far north of Scotland, just as the four-week dry spell came to an end. Things soon unravelled. After I descended from Canisp, I didn't feel strong enough to continue onto Ben More Assynt the same day, so I ended up ascending the latter the next day. When we returned to Penrith a few days later, I realised I was on the cusp of exhaustion. I had experienced a near-constant swaying sensation since Clisham and this had persisted ever since. In hindsight, rescheduling Sgùrr Dhòmhnuill during Phase Two was the first sign that I was tiring. Siobhan and I adjusted the portion sizes for all of my meals and this seemed to do the trick.
Climbing Beinn Eighe's screes  
© Simon Tull
As mentioned earlier, a significant proportion of Phase Three should have been plotted as single peak days. Now that I knew my capabilities, I imposed daily limits of 18 miles and/or 7,500ft of ascent as I reworked the itinerary for the five-week subsection. Over half of my upcoming hiking days became single peak days.
texts.6:
#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Phase Three resumed as we proceeded to work down the Scottish mainland. I endured the harshest conditions that I have ever been exposed to during my back-to-back ascents of An Teallach: Bidein a' Ghlas Thuill and Sgùrr Mòr in the Fannichs. Despite having hail and snow driven into me by gale-force winds between 50-60mph, I responded as I would do every other time I was faced with hardship during the challenge, by smiling and laughing to myself, for there was nowhere else I'd rather be. After scaling Sgorr Ruadh, my 60th P600 and the halfway milestone on day 45, I surprised Siobhan when we checked into the Cluanie Inn as a halfway treat for a couple of nights around a rest day. By now, I had realised that I could feasibly complete the challenge in around 100 days by early August.
Suitably rested, we meandered into some remote glens west of Loch Ness before venturing to the far end of Loch Arkaig. This is when my second setback occurred. I was supposed to ascend both Sgùrr na Cìche and Càrn Mòr as part of a mammoth route as they stand on opposite ends of Glen Dessarry (these are the only two P600s which can be reasonably combined). I summited the former and wandered to the base of the steep grassy slope that started the long traverse to Càrn Mòr. Realising that completing my route would take longer than anticipated and having no way of updating Siobhan as I was out of signal, the correct course was to leave Càrn Mòr for another time.
texts.7:
#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Whilst resting near Fort William, I reflected on the times when the isolation of hiking by myself on a tight schedule and in poor weather had begun to gnaw at me. I actually enjoy hiking in poor weather, so it was a telling sign as to how gruelling the conditions were. More so than any other point, I keenly felt the slow progress owing to the frequent single peak days, which, alongside the weather, made this stage of the challenge the least enjoyable. In spite of this, I never turned back. I have no profound answer as to how I managed to stay motivated. My overriding impulse was that the challenge was what I had always wanted, and it was not meant to be easy.
It was fitting that Ladhar Bheinn was the first P600 I scaled after skipping Càrn Mòr. The following week saw me work my way back towards Fort William. On Gulvain, I met Arran Evison, who had recently started his own challenge to be the youngest person to complete the Munros on a mountain bike. It was a timely encounter given my recent introspection and afterwards, I felt a renewed conviction about myself. We then headed to the Cairngorms, where my uncle joined me for Ben Macdui, the first time I had been accompanied on a hike during the challenge. On day 68, I reached my 80th P600, Beinn a' Ghlò: Càrn nan Gabhar, the 2/3 milestone.
The five-week subsection ended with Ben Alder, the most intimidating P600, given that a 26-mile route is required to reach the summit. Of course, I headed up in heavy rain! Crossing the Allt a'Bhealaich Bheithe was fraught as the river was heavily in spate. There were some rocks to hop over on my way out, but on my return, I simply waded through the waist-deep water. After five weeks away, I just wanted to get home.
Descending from Beinn an Lochain  
© Simon Tull
texts.8:
#### Phase Three – Scotland (Mainland)
Upon deciding that Saturday 26th July would be the final day of the challenge, I adjusted the rest of the itinerary. There were 34 P600s left, so it would be a push to ascend these in 19 days, but doing so would mean the challenge would have taken me 93 days, an achievement that originally I did not believe was possible.
The remaining 22 P600s in Phase Three were split between two blocks of six hiking days separated by a rest day. Càrn Mòr was one of the first P600s I ascended after returning to Scotland for the last time. A heatwave then settled in as I marched up Beinn a' Chreachain, during which I became the proud owner of around 30 swollen horsefly bites. Our final two days in Scotland each had a yellow weather warning forecast, one for heavy rain on Saturday and one for thunderstorms on Sunday. Neither materialised and despite the threat looming overhead, it was eerily calm as I stood atop Broad Law, my 82nd and final P600 in Scotland, exactly 10 weeks after summiting the first, Goat Fell.
In the following days, I had this feeling that the challenge actually ended on Broad Law. I can only put this down to two things. Up until the end of Phase Three, Siobhan and I had existed in an intense and tightly scheduled environment and although there were still 12 P600s left, Phase Four would be considerably more relaxed than what came before. Additionally, as I had strongly felt that the Scottish mainland was the real challenge for so long, in some ways, Phase Three had become "the" challenge.
Longside Edge from Skiddaw at golden hour  
© Simon Tull
texts.9:
#### Phase Four – England, the Isle of Man and Wales
_Monday 21st to Saturday 26th July_
I was supposed to rest on the Monday before diving into Phase Four, the final stretch across the 12 P600s in England, the Isle of Man and Wales. Instead, I brought Skiddaw forward to make the Tuesday less crammed, meaning that I would finish the challenge on a 12-day stint as my last rest day had been on Monday 14th July.
I was joined on Scafell Pike and Cross Fell by Alex Staniforth, fresh from his own challenge in which he set a new FKT of 43 days for the Nuttalls. Having scaled the P600s in England, we then made fleeting visits to the Isle of Man and the Brecon Beacons. It was poignant that Wales was the last country we visited as this is where my love of hillwalking was first nurtured. The challenge concluded with a pair of triple peak days in Snowdonia, the first of which began with Aran Fawddwy, the only P600 which had the distinction of me failing to ascend it (twice!) before. After a brisk ascent of Glyder Fawr, we met my family at the Snowdon Mountain Railway station in Llanberis and waited for some others to arrive.
I was humbled by everyone who chose to be there for Snowdon, my final P600. We started up the Llanberis Path and met Siobhan and my family who had taken the train. Holding Siobhan's hand, I took a moment to reflect before touching the trig point that crowns Snowdon. Following a swift descent to Llanberis, I stopped my watch.
The challenge was over.
Big team on Snowdon/Yr Wyddfa, the final P600  
© Simon Tull
texts.10:
#### Everyone loves fun facts, so here's a few about the challenge:
*   It took 93 days to complete (including 20 rest days)  
*   I hiked 923.1 miles / the equivalent of 35.2 marathons  
*   I ascended 359,154ft / the equivalent of 12.4 Mount Everests  
*   I am the 16th person known to have ascended the P600s  
*   I am only the second person known to have ascended the P600s in a single calendar year (the other is Liam Chase)  
*   I am the first person to complete the P600s in the six years since Liam  
*   I had only ascended 19 P600s before the challenge  
*   Besides setting a new FKT, I smashed Liam's record by 220 days. We're still friends!
It was a privilege to raise funds for both Mind Over Mountains and Every Life Matters. I am grateful for their support in raising awareness of the challenge that I was taking on to support them.
I doubt that I will directly inspire the next person who vies to set a quicker FKT for the P600s, but I hope they ask me to be there on their last peak to shake their hand when they do. Records are meant to be broken, so I am excited for when I am surpassed.
As for what's next, setting a new FKT for the P600s was very much a once in a lifetime feat. I intend to reascend the P600s during my lifetime and complete their classic routes. Maybe I'll be the first person to complete a second round...?
